title: Krishna Returns to Mathura
story:
The city knew they were coming before they arrived. For five nights the two sons of Vasudeva had traveled the road in the company of Damaghosha, keeping to the ways of a traveler, and word of them had run on ahead faster than their horses could carry it. By the time the walls of Mathura came into view, the whole city had risen to meet them.

Ugrasena came out first, at the head of the Yadavas. Behind him came the traders and the subjects and the ministers, and the boys and the old men, until it seemed no one had been left indoors. They had dressed the city as for a festival. At every crossing of the four streets they had hung garlands and raised flags; the trumpets sounded the note of joy, and the panegyrists went through the lanes singing the glories of the two brothers. The whole of Mathura, it is said, looked as delighted and as beautiful as on the day of Indra's festival. The singers called out along the highways: the two brothers Rama and Govinda, celebrated throughout the world, have arrived at their own city — go out and rejoice.

And their coming seemed to change the very air of the place. Where Rama and Krishna passed, no one in Mathura was poor, no one went about in soiled clothes, no one lay unconscious. The cows and the horses and the elephants grew glad, the birds began to sound auspicious notes, and men and women felt a quiet happiness they could not name. The winds that blew from the ten directions were clean of dust, and even the images of the gods in the temples seemed to brighten at their approach. People said that all the signs of the golden age, the Krita age, had appeared in Mathura with their coming.

Then, seated on a chariot drawn by fine horses, at an auspicious moment, Rama and Krishna entered the city. The Yadavas followed them as the gods follow Indra, and the two brothers, their faces full of gladness, passed like the sun and the moon entering a mountain into the house of their father Vasudeva. There they set aside their weapons of their own accord, and the burden of all they had carried fell away.

Before anything else, they bowed to their father's feet. Then they showed proper honor to king Ugrasena and to all the leading Yadavas gathered there. And the elders welcomed them in return with a warmth that asked nothing of them, and the brothers, light-hearted at last, went in to their mother's apartments. In the days that followed they stayed close to Ugrasena, and they lived in Mathura happily, at peace among their own people.
reflection: The homecoming is told almost entirely through what the city does and feels — the garlands, the clean winds, the auspicious birds — as if Mathura itself were a body returning to health. Krishna and Balarama are welcomed not with a victory parade but with a father's feet to bow to and a mother waiting inside, and that is where the long journey finally ends.
hero_scene: Rama and Krishna riding a chariot drawn by fine horses through the garlanded, flag-hung streets of Mathura, with Ugrasena and the Yadavas following them as the gods follow Indra, the whole city come out to greet them.
